confidence_note: The three-week app study with over 150 San Diego adults and the 'metabolic jetlag' idea are from Panda's 2015 Cell Metabolism paper and Salk release, which the book draws on; it was not checked against the book text itself, so confidence is medium. The old text's Nobel Prize, orchestra metaphor, shift-worker fat storage and 18-week mice claims were not verified and are dropped. Panda's book year is 2018 (June, Rodale hardcover), while the DB has 2019.
facts: Panda's group built a phone app so that people could photograph everything they ate and drank; each picture carried a time stamp.
More than 150 healthy adults aged 21 to 55, recruited in San Diego and not on a diet, did this for three weeks.
Most of them ate across 15 hours or longer each day.
Less than a quarter of daily calories came before noon, and over a third after 6 p.m.
The photos also showed patterns: coffee and milk in the morning, alcohol in the evening, tea all day, yogurt as a morning food, ice cream in the evening.
The authors proposed that irregular meal timing causes 'metabolic jetlag', with metabolic organs out of step with the body's clock.
Beyond meal timing, nearly two-thirds of participants took supplements or vitamins at times that varied from day to day, and medication timing varied too.
Volunteers were recruited through online and print ads in San Diego and had to come to the lab to sign consent; reminders went out about once a day.
There were no shift workers in the data; the authors said larger studies with shift workers are needed.
scene_details: time-stamped photo of every meal and drink
less than a quarter of calories before noon, over a third after 6 p.m.
tension: People who thought of themselves as eating three meals a day turned out to be eating across 15 hours or more.
opening_idea: Start with the time stamps on the photos and what they showed about when a normal day actually begins and ends.

lessons.idea: You can only fix your eating hours once you see them, so record them for a short stretch before changing anything.
lessons.anchor: Over 150 adults photographed every bite and drink and found they ate over 15 hours.
lessons.example: Someone who believes dinner is early might find, when they write it down, that snacks run until bedtime.

reflect_final: If you looked at time-stamped photos of everything you ate yesterday, when would your eating day have started and when would it have ended?

use_cases.situation: You wonder if your eating times are fine.
use_cases.move: Take a photo of everything you eat for a few days, as Panda's volunteers did, and read the first and last times.
Offer to compare when each of you first and last ate this week; the app study found most people spanned 15 hours or more.

use_cases.situation: A colleague asks about late dinners.
use_cases.move: Mention that Panda's study found over a third of calories came after 6 p.m., and ask when they usually stop eating.

pocket_idea: A time-stamped photo of each meal shows how long your eating day really is.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: People in Panda's app study ate across 15 hours or longer, with a third of calories after 6 p.m.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Panda's group asked over 150 San Diego adults to photograph everything they ate and drank for three weeks. Most ate across 15 hours or longer; less than a quarter of calories came before noon, over a third after 6 p.m. The authors call irregular eating times metabolic jetlag.
conversation_variants.question_idea: When does your eating day start and end?
